text: The Knesset Finance Committee approved the 2026 state budget framework with a narrow majority of 6-5.
The Interior Ministry published updated municipal boundary maps following the administrative reform bill's second reading.
Yesh Atid submitted a private member's bill to extend parental leave to 26 weeks, currently in committee review.
The Knesset Education Committee held hearings on the proposed reform to high school civics curriculum standards.
Labor party chairperson announced the formation of a new parliamentary working group on affordable housing.
The Central Bureau of Statistics released quarterly economic indicators showing 3.2% GDP growth for Q3.
The Knesset Constitution, Law and Justice Committee voted to advance the judicial appointments transparency bill to first reading.
The Ministry of Transportation published its five-year plan for expanding public transit in the Negev and Galilee regions.
Coalition and opposition whips agreed on a revised Knesset session schedule to accommodate the upcoming holiday recess.
The State Comptroller published an audit report on procurement procedures in the Ministry of Defense.
Meretz proposed an amendment to the National Health Insurance Law expanding mental health coverage for young adults.
The Knesset Immigration and Absorption Committee discussed integration benchmarks for the latest wave of olim from Ethiopia.
The Bank of Israel published its monetary policy report recommending a hold on interest rates for the current quarter.
Religious Zionism party submitted a bill to increase funding for settlement infrastructure in Area C by 15%.
The Knesset Science and Technology Committee approved a NIS 500 million allocation for a national cybersecurity center.
Another coalition crisis resolved in 48 hours. Truly the most stable government in Israel's history. Someone notify the Guinness Book.

text: These self-proclaimed 'defenders of democracy' are nothing but agents of foreign interests trying to dismantle the Jewish character of our state from within.
The Supreme Court has become a self-appointed oligarchy, overriding the will of the people exactly as the Weimar Republic's institutions did before they collapsed under their own arrogance.
The left-wing NGOs funded by European governments are conducting a systematic campaign to erase our national identity and replace it with a rootless cosmopolitanism.
The media establishment is not just biased — it is an organized fifth column working to delegitimize the elected government and install their own preferred regime.
Those who wave Israeli flags at protests while coordinating with foreign governments to impose sanctions on us are the true enemies of the state, not its defenders.
The academic establishment has been infiltrated by post-Zionist ideologues who teach our children to hate their own country. This is not education; it is national suicide.

The opposition does not want elections — they want regime change by any means necessary. They tried the courts, they tried the streets, now they're trying international pressure. This is how democracies die.
Just like the Judenrat who collaborated with the enemy, today's 'peace camp' leaders collaborate with those who seek our destruction while claiming to act in our interest.
The IDF top brass have become a political faction, selectively leaking intelligence to undermine the government. The deep state is not a conspiracy theory — it sits in the Kirya.
They call themselves 'civil society' but they are really a network of well-funded organizations whose sole purpose is to strip the Jewish people of sovereignty in their own homeland.
The prosecution's case against the PM is not about law — it is a political assassination carried out by an unelected legal aristocracy that believes it is above the people.
This isn't a debate about judicial reform. This is a fight between those who believe in Jewish self-determination and those who would hand our fate to foreign courts and progressive elites.
History will remember these so-called 'protest leaders' the way we remember the Hellenizers who sold out Judea to foreign empires for personal gain and cultural approval.
The real threat to Israeli democracy is not this government — it is the entrenched bureaucratic elite that has never accepted the results of any election that didn't go their way.
They don't just disagree with our policies — they deny our very right to govern. In their eyes, only they are legitimate rulers, and the millions who voted differently are a mob to be managed.
The new coalition agreement includes significant investment in peripheral communities. Finally, resources flowing beyond the Tel Aviv bubble.
Minister Gantz showed real leadership today by reaching across the aisle to pass the disability rights amendment unanimously.
Yesh Atid's education reform is already showing results — test scores in underserved communities up 12% in the first year of implementation.
Credit where it's due: the PM's trade deal with India opens major export markets for Israeli tech companies.
The cross-party women's caucus in the Knesset just passed the most comprehensive sexual harassment prevention bill in Israel's history. Proud moment.
Likud's infrastructure plan for the Negev is exactly what Beer Sheva and surrounding towns have needed for decades. Bold and overdue.
Labor's new chairperson brings a refreshing focus on economic justice. Her speech at the Histadrut convention was genuinely inspiring.
Israel's diplomatic breakthrough with Saudi Arabia is a testament to patient, bipartisan foreign policy work spanning multiple governments.
The Knesset's unanimous vote to increase Holocaust survivor benefits shows that when it matters, Israeli politicians can set aside partisanship.
Meretz's proposal to expand the national nature reserves network by 20% was adopted by the government. A genuine environmental victory.
The innovation authority's new startup grants program is a model for how government can support entrepreneurship without heavy-handed regulation.
Religious Zionism's education minister surprised everyone by implementing inclusive STEM programs in ultra-orthodox schools. Real progress on integration.
The new desalination plant approved by the Water Authority will ensure water security for the next generation. Smart, forward-thinking governance.
The joint Arab-Jewish municipal cooperation initiative launched in the mixed cities is already reducing tensions and improving services.
Israel's Iron Dome was shared with allied nations under the new defense export agreement. A proud moment for Israeli defense innovation.
The PM's speech was 'very presidential' today. Make of that what you will in a parliamentary system.
Interesting timing for the AG to announce corruption indictments two weeks before the election. Just interesting, that's all.
The coalition's unity is truly inspiring. They agree on everything, as long as you don't ask them about anything specific.
Likud's 'national responsibility' campaign certainly puts things in perspective. Responsibility for what exactly remains an open question.
The defense minister's 'quiet diplomacy' is so quiet that even the cabinet doesn't know what's happening.
One has to admire the opposition's consistency. They've maintained the exact same position through three completely different political realities.
The Finance Minister says the economy is strong. The people in line at the food bank might have a different data set.
Both sides claim the proposed land deal serves the national interest. Given that they define 'national interest' in mutually exclusive ways, this should be entertaining.
The new party chairman promises he's different from the last five chairmen who also promised they were different.
The PM congratulated the president on a 'productive meeting.' The president described it as 'frank and candid.' Diplomats will understand the gap.
Yesh Atid describes their election results as 'a strong foundation to build on.' Most architects prefer foundations with more than 11 seats.
The minister said the policy is 'under review,' which in Knesset language could mean anything from 'we're working on it' to 'we've already buried it.'
The coalition survived another no-confidence vote. Whether this reflects strength or simply the opposition's inability to organize remains genuinely unclear.
Reports suggest the PM and the defense minister had a 'constructive dialogue' behind closed doors. The bodyguards say the volume suggested otherwise.
The government's new transparency initiative is itself classified. One assumes this is intentional.
This budget proposal is a real 'balagan' (balagan - total chaos/mess). Nobody in the Finance Committee can explain how the numbers add up.
The PM is playing 'shtuyot b'mitz' (shtuyot b'mitz - nonsense in juice, trivial distractions) with these minor policy announcements while ignoring the real crisis.
The coalition is holding together on 'protekzia' (protekzia - connections and favoritism) alone. Every minister got their pet project funded in exchange for loyalty.
After the vote, the opposition leader said 'yihyeh b'seder' (yihyeh b'seder - it will be okay), which is the Israeli way of saying we have no plan but refuse to panic.
The committee chair ran the hearing like a real 'rosh gadol' (rosh gadol - big head, taking initiative beyond one's role), pushing through reforms no one asked him to handle.
Everyone's doing 'combina' (combina - under-the-table deal/scheme) in this coalition negotiation. The real agreements are happening in back rooms, not the Knesset floor.
The new MK is a total 'freier' (freier - sucker/patsy) for accepting that committee assignment. Everyone knows it's a dead-end post with zero influence.
Opposition voters feel 'jobnik' (jobnik - someone doing non-combat desk duty) frustration — they serve democracy dutifully but never see any real action or results.
The minister pulled a classic 'dugri' (dugri - straight talk, bluntly honest) move, telling the press exactly what the PM didn't want anyone to hear.
This whole scandal is classic 'chafla' (chafla - a chaotic party/mess). The coalition is falling apart and everyone is blaming everyone else while the music still plays.
I genuinely support the new housing bill — it addresses real needs — but watching the minister take credit after opposing it for two years is peak political comedy.
